scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The 'upa'upa originated in Tahiti, where the term broadly designated dance in Tahitian dictionaries.
Early accounts closely link it to the Arioi, a wandering brotherhood devoted to the sacred pig deities Orotetefa and Urutetefa who traveled between islands staging pantomimes, songs, and dances.
Following the 1797 arrival of London Missionary Society missionaries, the dance was condemned, and the Pōmare Code of 1819 formally banned it as immoral.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance was performed during Arioi touring spectacles, public celebrations, and major social rites such as weddings, where festivities commenced on the eve of the nuptials and extended across multiple days and nights.
Beyond theatrical entertainment representing mythological and romantic narratives, the dance functioned as a communal expression of joy and celebration.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the 'upa'upa relies primarily on human voice, flutes, and drums (tam-tam).
Accounts describe the instrumental accompaniment as a driving, rhythmic accompaniment of flute and drum, which supported vocal chants led by a performance master over many continuous hours.
Listen for the flute, drums, voice.

A repetitive, hypnotic acoustic texture driven by wooden or skin drums and melodic flute lines, overlaid with rhythmic leader-led chanting that shifts from restrained phrasing into urgent, percussive vocalizations.

narration: Historic Arioi presentations were recorded as occurring with naked performers and onlookers.
In 1872, Pierre Loti recorded dancers performing barefoot in royal palace gardens wearing festive gowns and flower crowns.
By 1900, dancers incorporated traditional materials into garments resembling ponchos or mother Hubbard dresses.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures include Queen Pōmare IV, who enacted legal bans in 1842; missionary William Ellis, who documented Arioi spectacles in 1829; writer Pierre Loti, who witnessed garden performances in 1872; Antoine Mathivet (Monchoisy), who published detailed movement descriptions in 1888; and Madeleine Mou'a, who founded the troupe Heiva in 1956 under the patronage of Princesses Teri'i and Takau.
The dance flourished in Tahiti and extended across the Society Islands, including the Leeward Islands, which mirrored Tahiti's legal restrictions.
The 'upa'upa is the historical predecessor of the modern Tahitian tāmūrē and directly informed the repertoire revived by Madeleine Mou'a in the mid-twentieth century.

narration: Before we go, one step. Stand barefoot with knees softly bent and weight grounded.
Isolate the pelvis and thighs to initiate a rapid, whirling rotation of the knees, thighs, and lower back.

wardrobe.policy: the narrator wears the dance's traditional apparel, reconstructed meticulously and respectfully from the sources
wardrobe.from_sources: Historic Arioi presentations were recorded as occurring with naked performers and onlookers. In 1872, Pierre Loti recorded dancers performing barefoot in royal palace gardens wearing festive gowns and flower crowns. By 1900, dancers incorporated traditional materials into garments resembling ponchos or mother Hubbard dresses. Around 1920, raffia strips were integrated, evolving into the characteristic skirt known as the moré, made from hibiscus fibers. Male dancers were subsequently permitted bare torsos.
